thread.title: General Electric's Fall From Grace: Don't Fret - General Electric Company (NYSE:GE)

author: Daniel Jones
title: General Electric's Fall From Grace: Don't Fret - General Electric Company (NYSE:GE)

organizations.name: index committee for s&p dow jones indices

text:
June 19th was a dark day in the history books for General Electric (NYSE: GE ). According to a press release issued by S&P Dow Jones Indices, a subsidiary of S&P Global, the conglomerate will be removed from the Dow Jones Industrial Average later this month. At first glance, some investors may see this as the embodiment of the business’s troubles, further proof that the future will only worsen for the once-grand American company, but when you really dig down deeper, this move is not only symbolic at best, it’s virtually immaterial to investors in the grand scheme of things.
General Electric’s fall from prominence In a letter to the public, David Blitzer, the Managing Director and Chairman of the Index Committee for S&P Dow Jones Indices, announced that, effective on the morning of June 26th, General Electric will no longer be considered a component of the Dow Jones Industrial Average. According to the press release, the business was one of the original members of the DJIA back when it was assembled in 1896, and it has remained on the list continuously since 1907.
The original DJIA components consisted not of 30 companies, but of 12, of which you can find a list of here . As the US transitioned away from being an industrial nation and focused more on services, the DJIA expanded and the original companies that comprised it rolled off. In fact, as of the time of this writing, only General Electric has remained on the list. Come June 26th, though, that will no longer be, as Walgreens Boots Alliance (NASDAQ: WBA ) will take its place.
There were two justifications given for S&P Dow Jones Indices’ decision. First and foremost is the continued evolution of the US economy. Today, companies that operate in the consumer, finance, healthcare, and technology spaces are more significant contributors to the economy than industrial stocks. While General Electric did generate $19.12 billion in revenue from its healthcare operations last year, and while the company does generate revenue from GE Capital and from various technologies, the disparity in size between the firm’s bits and pieces, and Walgreens, which generated $118.21 billion in sales last year, is clear.
The other reason relates to a simple word: price. Simply put, the DJIA is a price-weighted index, which means that companies with higher share prices have a larger impact on the DJIA’s trajectory than those with lower ones. Even though Walgreens has a market capitalization of $64.1 billion, a bit over half of the $112.5 billion market cap reported for General Electric, Walgreens’ share price is about five times greater than the $12.95 that General Electric recently closed at. Mr. Blitzer said it best when he stated that the conglomerate’s low share price means that it contributes less than one-half of one percent of the DJIA’s weight.
For those not familiar with the intricacies of the DJIA, overall market capitalization doesn’t matter. As you can see in the table below, companies included in the DJIA have market values ranging from between $34.6 billion (represented by Travelers Companies (NYSE: TRV )) and $912.7 billion ( Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL )). If the average were based on market value instead of share price, iconic American businesses like Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) with a market cap of $841.8 billion, Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) with a market cap of $818.7 billion, and Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A ) (NYSE: BRK.B ) with a market cap of $473.1 billion, would be included. They aren’t.
*Created by Author
This is symbolic, not substantive The first thought that flew to my mind when I heard of General Electric’s imminent departure from the DJIA was that it could have significant ramifications for market participants who own the stock. Surely, there is the reputational aspect of the move: a less-prominent enterprise would certainly attract less investor attention and there could be an initial slide in the share price of the firm because of it. But what about indices?
When companies get upgraded to indices, their share prices usually climb because in order to remain compliant with investment agreements, index funds, ETFs, and some mutual funds must allocate their assets in a way to track said financial instruments. Likewise, when companies are removed, their share prices tend to fall because there is mandated pressure to divest of the holdings in question in favor or whatever takes their place.
Interestingly, for General Electric, I don’t see this as all that likely and that’s because of one simple reason: nearly nobody buys into the Dow 30 stocks in index or ETF form. In an article published by CNBC last year, it was revealed that in the past 10 years, there were $302 billion worth of net inflows into index funds and ETFs that track the S&P 500. In the five years leading up to the article’s publication, net inflows totaled an impressive $236 billion. By their account, there were 152 such instruments.
By comparison, there were only five index funds and ETFs that tracked the DJIA, and total flows into them have been minuscule by comparison. Based on the article’s findings, in the prior 10 years there had been just $3 billion worth of net inflows into these funds, and in the five years leading up to that point there was actually a net outflow of $860 million. Though that’s still a sizable amount of money, total net inflows in the 10-year period covered amount to just 2.7% of General Electric’s existing market cap.
Takeaway The fact that General Electric is being booted from the DJIA is devastating reputationally. The conglomerate has now broken a 110-year streak of being included, and it’s the last of the old guard to leave. Absent a massive transformation in the company’s operations, it could be several years before it has a shot at being put on the list again, and more likely than not it will never be on that list as the US continues its move away from industrial operations and toward service-based ones. In reality, this is a huge embarrassment for management, but it’s more symbolic than it is substantive.
Given the psychological impact caused by the change, I suspect shares to fall in response to the news, but fundamentally it does not change anything. There will be no large exodus of major index funds and ETFs from the company and investors who were drawn to General Electric before this move should still like it, while those who dislike the company shouldn’t feel any better or worse about the change.
In fact, for investors who are long General Electric, any sort of decrease in share price caused by the transition should be capitalized on accordingly. If the conglomerate was an attractive purchase before this, it’s perhaps an even more attractive one after it.
